title: When hospitals build their own AI: a comparison of the EU and US regulatory framework.
paragraphs: Hospitals are increasingly developing their own artificial intelligence (AI) systems to address local clinical needs. In both the European Union (EU) and the USA, many of these systems qualify as AI-based medical devices but existing regulatory frameworks were primarily designed for commercially marketed products rather than hospital-developed AI.

This review provides the first comparative legal analysis of how the EU and the USA regulate hospital-developed AI. It shows that the EU explicitly recognises hospitals as regulated innovators through the Medical Device Regulation’s in-house exemption, whereas the USA largely regulates hospital-developed AI through general medical devices and software rules. The paper also identifies important differences in how each framework supports innovation, governance and the wider diffusion of successful AI systems.

The findings highlight the need for regulatory frameworks that both facilitate hospital innovation and ensure appropriate governance when locally developed AI systems are deployed more broadly. Future policy reforms should strengthen pathways for translating successful hospital-developed AI into safely scalable clinical tools while maintaining effective oversight.

Hospitals are no longer only purchasers of digital health technologies but are increasingly becoming developers of medical artificial intelligence (AI). Surveys show that in 2024, 80% of US hospitals used predictive AI sourced from their EHR developer, 52% used third-party developed AI and 50% used self-developed AI. 1 In Europe similar trends are emerging. 2 In both markets, commercial algorithms intended to apply to all settings might not be as adaptable or accurate across institutions because of differences in workflows, patient populations and local data distributions, 3 and may require extensive recalibration before they can be safely deployed in clinical practice.

The development of in-hospital AI systems—which we define as AI-based medical devices developed in a hospital facility (hereafter: Hospital-AI)—may permit hospitals to tailor models to local datasets and clinical needs and address clinically important problems that may attract limited commercial interest.

Although different in many ways, both the European Union (EU) and the USA regulate medical AI primarily through medical-device law, but they diverge in how they treat Hospital-AI systems. In the EU, the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) 4 provides a specific exemption for devices manufactured and used within health institutions, allowing certain Hospital-AI to operate outside the full conformity assessment regime. This creates uncertainty regarding how the AI Act and other regulations—such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the European Health Data Space (EHDS)—apply to such systems. In the USA, by contrast, Hospital-AI are, in principle, subject to the same regulatory framework as commercially marketed devices built outside hospitals when they meet the statutory definition of a medical device. This article compares EU and US approaches to Hospital-AI across three dimensions: responsiveness to clinical need, distribution of innovative capacity across healthcare institutions and pathways for scaling and deployment. It shows that both systems permit hospital-based innovation, but through different regulatory approaches—one that explicitly structures it through institutional obligations, and one that accommodates it within a more permissive and less differentiated framework. The EU expressly recognises hospitals as a distinct regulatory actor under the in-house device framework, while in the USA, Hospital-AI is largely governed by general device and software rules that do not differentiate hospitals from other developers.

We conducted a narrative legal review of the EU and the USA as leading jurisdictions where Hospital-AI is emerging under distinct regulatory models. On the EU side, we analyse the MDR and the AI Act, including guidance from the Medical Device Coordination Group and the AI Office/AI Board. On the US side, we examine the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA), as implemented by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), including the 21st Century Cures Act software exclusions and subsequent guidance on clinical decision support (CDS) and AI-enabled device software functions. We identify relevant scholarship through structured searches in PubMed, HeinOnline, Google Scholar and SSRN using terms such as “hospital developed AI,” “in-house medical devices,” and “AI medical device regulation,” and by hand-searching leading journals in health law, medical ethics and digital health. Our analysis covers legal and policy developments through August 2026 and does not include a systematic review of empirical studies on Hospital-AI.

Medical devices in the EU are governed primarily by the MDR. Under Article 2, the definition of medical device includes instruments or software intended for medical purposes, meaning that many clinical AI systems qualify as software medical devices and fall within the scope of the MDR. For these devices, the MDR sets comprehensive requirements for safety, performance, conformity assessment and post-market surveillance that all devices must meet before they can be marketed or used. Depending on their intended use—primarily defined by the manufacturer—devices are classified according to risk, ranging from class I (low risk) to class III (highest risk), ex Article 51. As disposed by Article 52 and recital 60, low-risk devices may often be self-certified by manufacturers, whereas higher-risk devices must undergo an independent conformity assessment by a notified body to verify compliance with MDR safety requirements.

Article 5(5) MDR provides an exception for Hospital-AI—manufactured and used exclusively within a health institution—allowing hospitals to develop and use such devices without undergoing the full conformity assessment procedures required for commercial products. 5 This exemption is intended to preserve the ability of hospitals and laboratories to develop bespoke solutions addressing specific clinical needs. 5

The in-house exemption applies under strict conditions: devices must be manufactured on a non-industrial scale and cannot be transferred to another legal entity; healthcare institutions must operate a quality management system governing design and manufacture, and demonstrate that patient needs cannot be met by an equivalent device available on the EU market. 6 Under MDCG 2023–1, institutions using the Article 5(5) route must maintain documentation describing the device’s design, manufacture and performance, and must demonstrate conformity with the MDR’s general safety and performance requirements in Annex I as well as implement postmarket surveillance and vigilance systems. 5 In practice, hospitals internalise many of the documentation and postmarket functions that would otherwise apply to CE-marked commercial devices and must provide documentation to national competent authorities on request. 7 These authorities—the regulatory bodies designated by each EU Member State to enforce medical device legislation—retain supervisory powers and may inspect compliance with Article 5(5). Failure to meet those conditions makes the device subject to re-review under the full MDR regime, including the usual enforcement tools available to competent authorities.

In addition to the MDR, the EU AI Act introduced a horizontal regulatory framework for AI systems across sectors, including healthcare, designed to address risks not fully covered by existing legislation. The AI Act adopts a risk-based approach, distinguishing prohibited AI practices, high-risk systems—subject to stringent requirements—and lower-risk systems subject to less stringent requirements and also introduces a regime for general-purpose AI models.

Under Article 6(1) of the AI Act, AI systems are classified as high-risk when they are products or safety components regulated under EU harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I—including the MDR—that require third-party conformity assessment. AI-enabled medical devices assessed by a notified body therefore automatically fall within the category of high-risk AI systems and, in addition to MDR requirements, must meet AI Act obligations on risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, traceability and human oversight. 8 Article 6(2) arguably provides a second route: AI systems listed in Annex III are also deemed high-risk. Annex III point 5(a) expressly includes AI used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public services ‘including healthcare services’, and point 5(d) covers AI used for triage and emergency dispatching. Hospital-AI deployed in public hospitals for admissions prioritisation, triage or eligibility scoring may therefore be high-risk under Article 6(2) irrespective of MDR mandated third-party assessment. 9 The application of these provisions to Hospital-AI nevertheless remains uncertain. The MDR might be considered to constitute lex specialis —a more specific set of rules that overrides the more general framework—governing the placing into service and use of in-hospital medical devices, so that the specific regulatory framework for health institutions should prevail when determining the applicable compliance pathway. This reading accords with the AI Act’s architecture, which generally treats existing sectoral product-safety legislation, including the MDR, as the primary regulatory framework for products already subject to harmonised EU safety rules. Recent legislative developments discussed below appear to favour the MDR-as-lex-specialis approach, under which the in-house status of the system remains the primary consideration, limiting the practical relevance of Annex III classification.

This regime creates a notable regulatory asymmetry when it comes to Hospital-AI and comparable AI-based devices developed outside the hospital. Because Article 5(5) MDR bypasses third-party conformity assessment, many Hospital-AI will not automatically qualify as high-risk AI and instead sit in the AI Act’s residual category outside the prohibited-practice, high-risk and specific transparency-obligation tiers. 10 In particular, this means that such devices will not be subject to the more intensive, independent checks on safety and performance that apply to high-risk AI systems, nor to the stricter transparency requirements designed to support oversight and accountability. Some provisions governing deployment remain relevant to both Hospital-AI and non-Hospital-AI: Article 4 on AI literacy applies irrespective of risk classification, 11 patient-facing tools may still trigger transparency duties under Article 50, and hospitals deploying AI systems under their own authority assume deployer obligations. Nevertheless, there are key differences creating a regulatory asymmetry between Hospital-AI and other AI-based medical devices. In particular, two AI systems performing the same clinical function may face materially different AI-law obligations depending on whether they are hospital-developed. Commercial devices subject to third-party conformity assessment under the MDR and classified as high-risk AI must comply with the AI Act’s full regime, while comparable in-house systems may avoid that classification and compliance. As a result, functionally similar tools may operate under different regulatory regimes, raising questions of regulatory coherence and potentially shaping incentives for how such systems are developed and deployed.

Since December 2025, two distinct EU reform tracks have affected this regulatory landscape. The Digital Omnibus on AI, initially proposed by the European Commission in November 2025, was enacted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 12 and entered into force on 27 July 2026. Separately, in December 2025, the Commission proposed amendments to the MDR and IVDR under COM(2025) 1023. As of August 2026, that proposal remains pending under the ordinary legislative procedure. 13 14

Four aspects of these reforms are particularly important for the regulatory analysis of Hospital-AI, although it is important to distinguish changes already enacted through the Digital Omnibus from those that remain proposed under the MDR/IVDR reform.

First, under the pending MDR/IVDR reform proposal, the MDR would move from Section A to Section B of Annex I of the AI Act. When high-risk classification under Article 6(1) is triggered via Section B, only Article 6(1) and the AI Act’s enforcement provisions (Articles 102–109 and 112) apply; the substantive AI-specific requirements in Articles 8–49—such as data governance, human oversight and cybersecurity—would be absorbed into the sectoral legislation. It is unclear whether the MDR—designed for hardware and relatively static software—can fully absorb safeguards for adaptive AI, and MDCG/AI Board guidance already notes that MDR does not explicitly address several AI-specific risks. 15 As one of us has argued elsewhere, shifting AI-specific obligations from the AI Act into an already stretched MDR framework risks returning medical AI oversight ‘back to square one’ by relying on instruments that were not designed with adaptive, data-driven systems in mind and that remain under-specified on AI-specific risks. 16

Second, the still pending reform package proposes amendments to Rule 11 of Annex VIII MDR, permitting a broader range of medical device software to be classified as Class I and thus to escape notified-body assessment. For AI medical devices, this would offer a direct route out of Article 6(1) high-risk classification, because Article 6(1)(b) would no longer be triggered. In our context, this would operate in parallel with the in-house pathway and in some respects go even further, as a mechanism by which hospital-developed AI can avoid high-risk status.

Third, the proposed amendments would make the in-house exemption more flexible, allowing in-house devices (including Hospital-AI) to be shared or moved between health institutions, where there is a duly justified interest of public health or patient safety or health. 13 17

Finally, the Digital Omnibus has now postponed the application of the AI Act’s high-risk requirements for systems falling within Article 6(1), including qualifying AI-enabled medical devices, until 2 August 2028. 12 During this transitional period, AI-based medical devices continue to operate under the MDR before the relevant AI Act high-risk requirements become applicable. European stakeholders have argued that the MDR implementation already threatens the availability of some essential devices and diagnostic tests. 18 In this setting, in-house development can help maintain clinical capacity where commercial supply is constrained, but it also tests whether a framework built mainly around internal control remains adequate as the in-house pathway gains importance.

Unlike the EU framework, US law does not provide a specific exemption for Hospital-AI. Hospital-AI that meet the statutory definition of a medical device are therefore, in principle, subject to the same regulatory requirements as commercially marketed products. In practice, however, many such systems may fall outside the FDA’s core regulatory framework if they qualify for the software exclusions introduced by the 21st Century Cures Act. Even if outside the exclusion, they may face relatively limited oversight when cleared through the 510(k) pathway.

Medical devices in the USA are regulated by the FDA under the FDCA. The Act defines a medical device broadly as an instrument, apparatus, implement, machine […] or other similar or related article, including any component, part or accessory, intended for the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of disease (Section 201(h)(1)) and classifies devices into three risk-based categories (Class I–III). Most medical devices require some form of premarket review before entering the market, either through premarket approval (PMA)—which requires manufacturers to demonstrate the device’s safety and effectiveness based on clinical and technical evidence—or through the 510(k) notification pathway, under which manufacturers must show that the device is substantially equivalent to an existing device already on the market, a process generally considered less demanding and sometimes reliant on older predicate technologies. Software intended for medical purposes—including AI-based devices—may qualify as Software as a Medical Device when it performs medical functions without being part of a hardware medical device. 19 – 21

The regulatory reach of the FDA over medical AI was significantly narrowed by the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, which amended the FDCA to exclude certain software functions from the definition of a medical device. In particular, under Section 520(o)(1)(E), some CDS software is excluded where it displays or analyses medical information and provides recommendations to healthcare professionals, provided that it does not acquire, process or analyse medical images or signals and that it ‘enables such healthcare professional to independently review the basis for such recommendations’ and does not promote primary reliance on its outputs. The recent FDA guidance clarifies that, to meet this threshold, the software must provide sufficient information about the data sources, logic and performance underlying its recommendations to allow independent clinical judgement. 22 As a result, a range of AI-based clinical tools falls outside FDA oversight. 23

As for specific intervention in the AI space, more recently, the FDA has operationalised the Total Product Life Cycle (TPLC) oversight model through a series of updated guidance documents. Its 2025 draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions emphasises a comprehensive lifecycle approach to risk management, integrating premarket evaluation with ongoing postmarket performance monitoring to address the adaptive nature of AI systems. 24 25

A central component of this framework is the use of predetermined change control plans (PCCPs), which were formalised in final FDA guidance as further elaborated in 2025. 26 These plans allow manufacturers to implement prespecified algorithm modifications without submitting a new marketing application, provided that the changes fall within an approved scope and maintain safety and effectiveness.

However, among the already very limited number of AI-based medical devices subject to FDA oversight, most are authorised through the 510(k) pathway. As a result, many such systems fall outside more comprehensive lifecycle regulatory approaches, including TPLC oversight and PCCPs.

In sum, as compared with the EU approach, US law regulates software functions rather than the institutional context in which they are developed. As a result, hospital-developed AI is not treated as a distinct regulatory category but instead falls within the broader legal regime governing medical software and CDS. Hospital innovation therefore appears largely as a by-product of general software regulation rather than as a specifically targeted site of clinical innovation.

These structural differences shape how Hospital-AI systems emerge, are governed within clinical settings, and ultimately move—or fail to move—beyond the institutions in which they are created. When it comes to hospital-developed AI, three related objectives for regulation stand out: it should enable hospitals to respond to pressing clinical needs, support innovation within local clinical environments and permit the safe and useful diffusion of successful systems beyond the institutions in which they originate. The following section examines these dimensions in turn, focusing on how each regulatory model organises the relationship between local experimentation and system-wide diffusion.

Flexibility to develop AI tools in response to clinical needs exists in both the EU and US frameworks, but it is embedded through fundamentally different regulatory architectures. In the EU, the in-house exemption under Article 5(5) MDR explicitly recognises hospitals as a distinct category of innovator and creates a calibrated space for this type of development. By removing full conformity assessment, the exemption reduces regulatory friction and avoids congestion that—because of the complex EU regulatory framework—would otherwise delay the deployment of locally needed tools. 27

Crucially, however, this flexibility exists alongside some requirements—to demonstrate that no equivalent device is available on the market, implement a quality management system and document compliance with general safety and performance requirements—which embed a form of internalised regulatory governance. In other words, regulatory oversight is not removed but relocated, requiring hospitals to assume functions—such as validation, risk management and documentation—that would otherwise be performed by external regulators.

In the USA, as discussed in previous paragraphs, many clinical AI systems fall outside FDA oversight altogether due to the statutory exclusions introduced by the 21st Century Cures Act and subsequent guidance, while others are subject only to relatively limited scrutiny through pathways such as 510(k) clearance. Tort liability, in theory, provides an ex post form of pressure to develop safe products, but patients face significant challenges in lawsuits against developers of medical AI. 28 These factors result in a permissive environment in the USA in which hospital-developed tools can be developed with comparatively low ex ante regulatory barriers. Unlike the EU approach, this flexibility is not grounded in an explicit recognition of hospitals as a distinct regulatory category. Instead, Section 520(o)(1)(A) and (E) exclusions turn on what the software does and how it is used in clinical practice—such as supporting, rather than replacing, professional judgement—rather than on who developed it. Hospital-AI systems are therefore effectively ‘swept along’ by a broader framework that narrows the scope of regulated software functions based on use, not origin, in the US framework. With the possible exception of data acquisition, where the main US federal health privacy law, HIPAA, gives hospitals more leeway in using data they themselves collect from patients and do not leave the ‘covered entity’, the US approach does not seek to treat the hospital system as a unique site for AI regulation.

A second point of comparison concerns the distribution of innovative capacity across healthcare systems. In both the EU and the USA, the ability to develop, validate, and sustain hospital-based AI is likely to cluster in large academic medical centres and technologically advanced institutions with access to high-quality data infrastructure, technical expertise, governance capacity and financial resources. 29 30 To be fair, this pattern is not unique to Hospital-AI and should not be attributed solely to the regulatory design choices; in other forms of medical innovation, development tends to also concentrate in leading institutions before diffusing more broadly. 31 32 Regulatory choices can, however, amplify, mitigate, or leave unchanged this dynamic.

Concentration in leading institutions is not inherently undesirable. Large academic medical centres often possess the clinical volume, technical expertise, data and governance structures necessary to develop and safely test novel AI systems. The concern, therefore, is not concentration as such, but concentration without effective diffusion. Problems arise when the institutions that can develop these systems are also the primary beneficiaries because successful tools do not easily travel beyond their walls. In that situation, three related risks emerge: first, that only well-resourced institutions are able to develop Hospital-AI; second, that those institutions are also the primary beneficiaries if such systems remain difficult to adopt beyond their walls; and third, that systems trained in a narrow set of settings may perform less reliably in more diverse clinical environments. For the purposes of this article, the central concern is whether the benefits of innovation diffuse equitably across sites of deployment rather than where innovation occurs per se. Although a more equitable distribution of innovative capacity may be desirable, concentration in the site of innovation is less problematic when there is equitable distribution in sites of deployment over relatively short time horizons.

On the first problem, that only well-resourced institutions can develop Hospital-AI, the difference in regulatory frameworks discussed above likely plays only a modest role. Even without the health-institution exception in the EU, innovation would probably remain concentrated in well-resourced hospitals because the key drivers—technical expertise, data access and institutional investment—are largely independent of Article 5(5) MDR. At most, the exception may reinforce an existing pattern by giving already capable institutions a feasible route to develop and deploy local AI tools without bearing the full costs of conformity assessment. Institutions that already possess the expertise and compliance infrastructure needed to satisfy its conditions are better positioned both to develop such systems and to benefit from their initial use than hospitals with fewer resources.

In some ways, the fact that Hospital-AI development also clusters in large academic medical centres in the USA, where there is no preferential regulatory treatment for Hospital-AI, proves the point. The same structural constraints that limit internal development—technical expertise, data infrastructure and governance capacity—also complicate the procurement, evaluation and safe integration of third-party systems, even though building tools locally is generally the more demanding task.

Turning to the second and third concerns identified above, the distributional implications of Hospital-AI innovation depend not only on who develops these systems but also on how easily they can be adopted by other institutions. Deploying a system in a new institution often requires adapting it to local data pipelines, electronic health record architectures, clinical workflows and governance structures, as well as evaluating how the model performs in a different data environment.

These challenges are mitigated when systems are accompanied by documentation describing the model architecture, training data, validation procedures and technical requirements. The portability of Hospital-AI depends not only on the technical artefact itself but also on the transparency of the information that travels with it. Where such documentation is available, receiving hospitals can assess how a system should be integrated into local infrastructure and whether it is appropriate for their patient population.

Within the EU, devices that move beyond the in-house exception must undergo conformity assessment and be supported by technical documentation allowing external institutions to evaluate their safety and performance. However, the proposed modifications to the MDR could allow certain Hospital-AI systems to circulate among affiliated institutions without undergoing the same procedures, raising renewed questions about adaptability and oversight.

In the USA, similar transparency is sometimes provided through so-called model cards describing intended use, training data, evaluation metrics and model limitations. For example, initiatives such as the CHAI Applied Model Card propose detailed, standardised documentation of an AI system’s purpose, performance, risks and context of use. 33

In the EU, tools developed under the health-institution exception benefit from a tailored internal-use regime that dispenses with full conformity assessment while imposing institutional governance requirements. Once they move beyond that space, they generally become subject to the full product-regulatory framework, including notified body assessment under the MDR and where applicable, AI Act obligations—which include additional requirements for the manufacturer to satisfy. This creates a discontinuous pathway from experimentation to diffusion: systems initially facilitated as Hospital-AI may later encounter a steep increase in procedural, evidentiary and organisational demands, as highlighted by Pesapane et al. 7

This discontinuity may serve an important function by enabling hospitals to respond to clinical needs, generate real-world experience and build evidence before assuming the full cost of regulatory compliance. The in-house pathway thus functions as regulatory scaffolding, enabling early experimentation under lighter ex ante constraints. In this respect, it resembles regulatory sandboxes—such as those introduced by the AI Act—but lacks the structured mechanisms for regulatory learning, iterative oversight or staged transition to broader deployment. 34 In this sense, the in-house regime resembles a ‘sandbox without sandbox mechanisms’. AI Act sandboxes under Article 57 are time-limited, operate under explicit supervisory arrangements and are designed to generate insights that can inform both regulatory practice and future rule-making. By contrast, the in-house pathway is more permanent and primarily governed by internal institutional processes. This may discourage scaling or incentivise continued reliance on in-house status, even where broader deployment would be clinically beneficial.

US law does not create a distinct regulatory grammar for Hospital-AI comparable to the European in-house exemption. Instead, Hospital-AI either falls within existing FDA device pathways—such as 510(k), De Novo or PMA—or, in many cases, remains outside the device framework altogether due to the software exclusions introduced by the 21st Century Cures Act. As a result, there is no clearly defined regulatory transition between internal clinical use and wider deployment analogous to the shift that occurs under the EU in-house regime.

This does not necessarily mean that diffusion is easier in the US context. Where systems fall outside the FDA device framework, their development and initial use may face relatively limited ex ante regulatory barriers. At the same time, the absence of formal authorisation pathways for many such tools may also reduce the availability of standardised signals of safety, effectiveness and quality that could facilitate broader adoption across institutions. Diffusion of Hospital-AI may therefore depend more on institutional trust, local validation and informal knowledge transfer than on regulatory transition points.

In both jurisdictions, the pathway from early hospital experimentation to wider clinical diffusion remains underdeveloped. Even where local innovation is facilitated, neither framework provides clear mechanisms for translating successful hospital-developed systems into tools that can be reliably adopted across heterogeneous healthcare environments. Absent better-defined mechanisms to support this transition, hospital-developed AI may remain confined to its originating institutions, even where broader deployment might be clinically desirable.

Comparing the current regulatory approaches still reveals a deep divergence between designed regulatory accommodation in the EU and incidental regulatory permissiveness in the USA. In the EU, hospitals are explicitly recognised as regulatory actors and flexibility is structured through institutional obligations. In the USA, by contrast, hospital-developed AI largely operates within a general regulatory framework that does not directly address its institutional context.

As indicated in the above, the significance of this divergence is likely to become more apparent as both systems evolve. Ongoing reforms in the EU, alongside the still fragmented and developing AI governance landscape in the USA, will test whether structured institutional oversight translates into more consistent and accountable use, or whether more permissive approaches better support timely development and diffusion. Our argument has, self-consciously, focused on regulatory design choices and possible implications not outcomes. This article does not provide empirical evidence that either regulatory model causes better real-world clinical, innovation or diffusion outcomes. The empirical basis for assessing these trade-offs remains limited. Comparative evidence on the volume, development timelines, governance practices and clinical performance of hospital-developed AI systems, as well as on the pathways through which such systems diffuse beyond their originating institutions, would be useful to inform the picture. Even with such evidence, isolating the causal effects of regulatory design from other differences—hospital organisation, reimbursement and national health policy—would remain difficult. Still, reflecting on the underlying design choices helps clarify what each system is trying to accomplish.

What is clear is that regulatory recognition of hospitals as a distinct actor is a consequential design choice. The central challenge for policymakers is therefore not only how much flexibility to allow but how to ensure that such flexibility is meaningfully governed as innovation increasingly originates within healthcare systems themselves. This may require, for example, clearer documentation and transparency obligations for in-house systems, more structured pathways for transitioning successful tools from internal use to broader deployment and more explicit oversight where hospital-developed systems begin to circulate across institutions.

The MDR might be considered to constitute lex specialis —a more specific set of rules that overrides the more general framework—governing the placing into service and use of in-hospital medical devices, so that the specific regulatory framework for health institutions should prevail when determining the applicable compliance pathway. This reading accords with the AI Act’s architecture, which generally treats existing sectoral product-safety legislation, including the MDR, as the primary regulatory framework for products already subject to harmonised EU safety rules. Recent legislative developments discussed below appear to favour the MDR-as-lex-specialis approach, under which the in-house status of the system remains the primary consideration, limiting the practical relevance of Annex III classification.

This regime creates a notable regulatory asymmetry when it comes to Hospital-AI and comparable AI-based devices developed outside the hospital. Because Article 5(5) MDR bypasses third-party conformity assessment, many Hospital-AI will not automatically qualify as high-risk AI and instead sit in the AI Act’s residual category outside the prohibited-practice, high-risk and specific transparency-obligation tiers. 10 In particular, this means that such devices will not be subject to the more intensive, independent checks on safety and performance that apply to high-risk AI systems, nor to the stricter transparency requirements designed to support oversight and accountability. Some provisions governing deployment remain relevant to both Hospital-AI and non-Hospital-AI: Article 4 on AI literacy applies irrespective of risk classification, 11 patient-facing tools may still trigger transparency duties under Article 50, and hospitals deploying AI systems under their own authority assume deployer obligations. Nevertheless, there are key differences creating a regulatory asymmetry between Hospital-AI and other AI-based medical devices. In particular, two AI systems performing the same clinical function may face materially different AI-law obligations depending on whether they are hospital-developed. Commercial devices subject to third-party conformity assessment under the MDR and classified as high-risk AI must comply with the AI Act’s full regime, while comparable in-house systems may avoid that classification and compliance. As a result, functionally similar tools may operate under different regulatory regimes, raising questions of regulatory coherence and potentially shaping incentives for how such systems are developed and deployed.

Since December 2025, two distinct EU reform tracks have affected this regulatory landscape. The Digital Omnibus on AI, initially proposed by the European Commission in November 2025, was enacted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 12 and entered into force on 27 July 2026. Separately, in December 2025, the Commission proposed amendments to the MDR and IVDR under COM(2025) 1023. As of August 2026, that proposal remains pending under the ordinary legislative procedure. 13 14

Four aspects of these reforms are particularly important for the regulatory analysis of Hospital-AI, although it is important to distinguish changes already enacted through the Digital Omnibus from those that remain proposed under the MDR/IVDR reform.

First, under the pending MDR/IVDR reform proposal, the MDR would move from Section A to Section B of Annex I of the AI Act. When high-risk classification under Article 6(1) is triggered via Section B, only Article 6(1) and the AI Act’s enforcement provisions (Articles 102–109 and 112) apply; the substantive AI-specific requirements in Articles 8–49—such as data governance, human oversight and cybersecurity—would be absorbed into the sectoral legislation. It is unclear whether the MDR—designed for hardware and relatively static software—can fully absorb safeguards for adaptive AI, and MDCG/AI Board guidance already notes that MDR does not explicitly address several AI-specific risks. 15 As one of us has argued elsewhere, shifting AI-specific obligations from the AI Act into an already stretched MDR framework risks returning medical AI oversight ‘back to square one’ by relying on instruments that were not designed with adaptive, data-driven systems in mind and that remain under-specified on AI-specific risks. 16

Second, the still pending reform package proposes amendments to Rule 11 of Annex VIII MDR, permitting a broader range of medical device software to be classified as Class I and thus to escape notified-body assessment. For AI medical devices, this would offer a direct route out of Article 6(1) high-risk classification, because Article 6(1)(b) would no longer be triggered. In our context, this would operate in parallel with the in-house pathway and in some respects go even further, as a mechanism by which hospital-developed AI can avoid high-risk status.

Third, the proposed amendments would make the in-house exemption more flexible, allowing in-house devices (including Hospital-AI) to be shared or moved between health institutions, where there is a duly justified interest of public health or patient safety or health. 13 17

Finally, the Digital Omnibus has now postponed the application of the AI Act’s high-risk requirements for systems falling within Article 6(1), including qualifying AI-enabled medical devices, until 2 August 2028. 12 During this transitional period, AI-based medical devices continue to operate under the MDR before the relevant AI Act high-risk requirements become applicable. European stakeholders have argued that the MDR implementation already threatens the availability of some essential devices and diagnostic tests. 18 In this setting, in-house development can help maintain clinical capacity where commercial supply is constrained, but it also tests whether a framework built mainly around internal control remains adequate as the in-house pathway gains importance.

Unlike the EU framework, US law does not provide a specific exemption for Hospital-AI. Hospital-AI that meet the statutory definition of a medical device are therefore, in principle, subject to the same regulatory requirements as commercially marketed products. In practice, however, many such systems may fall outside the FDA’s core regulatory framework if they qualify for the software exclusions introduced by the 21st Century Cures Act. Even if outside the exclusion, they may face relatively limited oversight when cleared through the 510(k) pathway.

Medical devices in the USA are regulated by the FDA under the FDCA. The Act defines a medical device broadly as an instrument, apparatus, implement, machine […] or other similar or related article, including any component, part or accessory, intended for the diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention of disease (Section 201(h)(1)) and classifies devices into three risk-based categories (Class I–III). Most medical devices require some form of premarket review before entering the market, either through premarket approval (PMA)—which requires manufacturers to demonstrate the device’s safety and effectiveness based on clinical and technical evidence—or through the 510(k) notification pathway, under which manufacturers must show that the device is substantially equivalent to an existing device already on the market, a process generally considered less demanding and sometimes reliant on older predicate technologies. Software intended for medical purposes—including AI-based devices—may qualify as Software as a Medical Device when it performs medical functions without being part of a hardware medical device. 19 – 21

The regulatory reach of the FDA over medical AI was significantly narrowed by the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, which amended the FDCA to exclude certain software functions from the definition of a medical device. In particular, under Section 520(o)(1)(E), some CDS software is excluded where it displays or analyses medical information and provides recommendations to healthcare professionals, provided that it does not acquire, process or analyse medical images or signals and that it ‘enables such healthcare professional to independently review the basis for such recommendations’ and does not promote primary reliance on its outputs. The recent FDA guidance clarifies that, to meet this threshold, the software must provide sufficient information about the data sources, logic and performance underlying its recommendations to allow independent clinical judgement. 22 As a result, a range of AI-based clinical tools falls outside FDA oversight. 23

As for specific intervention in the AI space, more recently, the FDA has operationalised the Total Product Life Cycle (TPLC) oversight model through a series of updated guidance documents. Its 2025 draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions emphasises a comprehensive lifecycle approach to risk management, integrating premarket evaluation with ongoing postmarket performance monitoring to address the adaptive nature of AI systems. 24 25

A central component of this framework is the use of predetermined change control plans (PCCPs), which were formalised in final FDA guidance as further elaborated in 2025. 26 These plans allow manufacturers to implement prespecified algorithm modifications without submitting a new marketing application, provided that the changes fall within an approved scope and maintain safety and effectiveness.

However, among the already very limited number of AI-based medical devices subject to FDA oversight, most are authorised through the 510(k) pathway. As a result, many such systems fall outside more comprehensive lifecycle regulatory approaches, including TPLC oversight and PCCPs.

In sum, as compared with the EU approach, US law regulates software functions rather than the institutional context in which they are developed. As a result, hospital-developed AI is not treated as a distinct regulatory category but instead falls within the broader legal regime governing medical software and CDS. Hospital innovation therefore appears largely as a by-product of general software regulation rather than as a specifically targeted site of clinical innovation.

These structural differences shape how Hospital-AI systems emerge, are governed within clinical settings, and ultimately move—or fail to move—beyond the institutions in which they are created. When it comes to hospital-developed AI, three related objectives for regulation stand out: it should enable hospitals to respond to pressing clinical needs, support innovation within local clinical environments and permit the safe and useful diffusion of successful systems beyond the institutions in which they originate. The following section examines these dimensions in turn, focusing on how each regulatory model organises the relationship between local experimentation and system-wide diffusion.

Flexibility to develop AI tools in response to clinical needs exists in both the EU and US frameworks, but it is embedded through fundamentally different regulatory architectures. In the EU, the in-house exemption under Article 5(5) MDR explicitly recognises hospitals as a distinct category of innovator and creates a calibrated space for this type of development. By removing full conformity assessment, the exemption reduces regulatory friction and avoids congestion that—because of the complex EU regulatory framework—would otherwise delay the deployment of locally needed tools. 27

Crucially, however, this flexibility exists alongside some requirements—to demonstrate that no equivalent device is available on the market, implement a quality management system and document compliance with general safety and performance requirements—which embed a form of internalised regulatory governance. In other words, regulatory oversight is not removed but relocated, requiring hospitals to assume functions—such as validation, risk management and documentation—that would otherwise be performed by external regulators.

In the USA, as discussed in previous paragraphs, many clinical AI systems fall outside FDA oversight altogether due to the statutory exclusions introduced by the 21st Century Cures Act and subsequent guidance, while others are subject only to relatively limited scrutiny through pathways such as 510(k) clearance. Tort liability, in theory, provides an ex post form of pressure to develop safe products, but patients face significant challenges in lawsuits against developers of medical AI. 28 These factors result in a permissive environment in the USA in which hospital-developed tools can be developed with comparatively low ex ante regulatory barriers. Unlike the EU approach, this flexibility is not grounded in an explicit recognition of hospitals as a distinct regulatory category. Instead, Section 520(o)(1)(A) and (E) exclusions turn on what the software does and how it is used in clinical practice—such as supporting, rather than replacing, professional judgement—rather than on who developed it. Hospital-AI systems are therefore effectively ‘swept along’ by a broader framework that narrows the scope of regulated software functions based on use, not origin, in the US framework. With the possible exception of data acquisition, where the main US federal health privacy law, HIPAA, gives hospitals more leeway in using data they themselves collect from patients and do not leave the ‘covered entity’, the US approach does not seek to treat the hospital system as a unique site for AI regulation.

A second point of comparison concerns the distribution of innovative capacity across healthcare systems. In both the EU and the USA, the ability to develop, validate, and sustain hospital-based AI is likely to cluster in large academic medical centres and technologically advanced institutions with access to high-quality data infrastructure, technical expertise, governance capacity and financial resources. 29 30 To be fair, this pattern is not unique to Hospital-AI and should not be attributed solely to the regulatory design choices; in other forms of medical innovation, development tends to also concentrate in leading institutions before diffusing more broadly. 31 32 Regulatory choices can, however, amplify, mitigate, or leave unchanged this dynamic.

Concentration in leading institutions is not inherently undesirable. Large academic medical centres often possess the clinical volume, technical expertise, data and governance structures necessary to develop and safely test novel AI systems. The concern, therefore, is not concentration as such, but concentration without effective diffusion. Problems arise when the institutions that can develop these systems are also the primary beneficiaries because successful tools do not easily travel beyond their walls. In that situation, three related risks emerge: first, that only well-resourced institutions are able to develop Hospital-AI; second, that those institutions are also the primary beneficiaries if such systems remain difficult to adopt beyond their walls; and third, that systems trained in a narrow set of settings may perform less reliably in more diverse clinical environments. For the purposes of this article, the central concern is whether the benefits of innovation diffuse equitably across sites of deployment rather than where innovation occurs per se. Although a more equitable distribution of innovative capacity may be desirable, concentration in the site of innovation is less problematic when there is equitable distribution in sites of deployment over relatively short time horizons.

On the first problem, that only well-resourced institutions can develop Hospital-AI, the difference in regulatory frameworks discussed above likely plays only a modest role. Even without the health-institution exception in the EU, innovation would probably remain concentrated in well-resourced hospitals because the key drivers—technical expertise, data access and institutional investment—are largely independent of Article 5(5) MDR. At most, the exception may reinforce an existing pattern by giving already capable institutions a feasible route to develop and deploy local AI tools without bearing the full costs of conformity assessment. Institutions that already possess the expertise and compliance infrastructure needed to satisfy its conditions are better positioned both to develop such systems and to benefit from their initial use than hospitals with fewer resources.

In some ways, the fact that Hospital-AI development also clusters in large academic medical centres in the USA, where there is no preferential regulatory treatment for Hospital-AI, proves the point. The same structural constraints that limit internal development—technical expertise, data infrastructure and governance capacity—also complicate the procurement, evaluation and safe integration of third-party systems, even though building tools locally is generally the more demanding task.

Turning to the second and third concerns identified above, the distributional implications of Hospital-AI innovation depend not only on who develops these systems but also on how easily they can be adopted by other institutions. Deploying a system in a new institution often requires adapting it to local data pipelines, electronic health record architectures, clinical workflows and governance structures, as well as evaluating how the model performs in a different data environment.

These challenges are mitigated when systems are accompanied by documentation describing the model architecture, training data, validation procedures and technical requirements. The portability of Hospital-AI depends not only on the technical artefact itself but also on the transparency of the information that travels with it. Where such documentation is available, receiving hospitals can assess how a system should be integrated into local infrastructure and whether it is appropriate for their patient population.

Within the EU, devices that move beyond the in-house exception must undergo conformity assessment and be supported by technical documentation allowing external institutions to evaluate their safety and performance. However, the proposed modifications to the MDR could allow certain Hospital-AI systems to circulate among affiliated institutions without undergoing the same procedures, raising renewed questions about adaptability and oversight.

In the USA, similar transparency is sometimes provided through so-called model cards describing intended use, training data, evaluation metrics and model limitations. For example, initiatives such as the CHAI Applied Model Card propose detailed, standardised documentation of an AI system’s purpose, performance, risks and context of use. 33

In the EU, tools developed under the health-institution exception benefit from a tailored internal-use regime that dispenses with full conformity assessment while imposing institutional governance requirements. Once they move beyond that space, they generally become subject to the full product-regulatory framework, including notified body assessment under the MDR and where applicable, AI Act obligations—which include additional requirements for the manufacturer to satisfy. This creates a discontinuous pathway from experimentation to diffusion: systems initially facilitated as Hospital-AI may later encounter a steep increase in procedural, evidentiary and organisational demands, as highlighted by Pesapane et al. 7

This discontinuity may serve an important function by enabling hospitals to respond to clinical needs, generate real-world experience and build evidence before assuming the full cost of regulatory compliance. The in-house pathway thus functions as regulatory scaffolding, enabling early experimentation under lighter ex ante constraints. In this respect, it resembles regulatory sandboxes—such as those introduced by the AI Act—but lacks the structured mechanisms for regulatory learning, iterative oversight or staged transition to broader deployment. 34 In this sense, the in-house regime resembles a ‘sandbox without sandbox mechanisms’. AI Act sandboxes under Article 57 are time-limited, operate under explicit supervisory arrangements and are designed to generate insights that can inform both regulatory practice and future rule-making. By contrast, the in-house pathway is more permanent and primarily governed by internal institutional processes. This may discourage scaling or incentivise continued reliance on in-house status, even where broader deployment would be clinically beneficial.

US law does not create a distinct regulatory grammar for Hospital-AI comparable to the European in-house exemption. Instead, Hospital-AI either falls within existing FDA device pathways—such as 510(k), De Novo or PMA—or, in many cases, remains outside the device framework altogether due to the software exclusions introduced by the 21st Century Cures Act. As a result, there is no clearly defined regulatory transition between internal clinical use and wider deployment analogous to the shift that occurs under the EU in-house regime.

This does not necessarily mean that diffusion is easier in the US context. Where systems fall outside the FDA device framework, their development and initial use may face relatively limited ex ante regulatory barriers. At the same time, the absence of formal authorisation pathways for many such tools may also reduce the availability of standardised signals of safety, effectiveness and quality that could facilitate broader adoption across institutions. Diffusion of Hospital-AI may therefore depend more on institutional trust, local validation and informal knowledge transfer than on regulatory transition points.

In both jurisdictions, the pathway from early hospital experimentation to wider clinical diffusion remains underdeveloped. Even where local innovation is facilitated, neither framework provides clear mechanisms for translating successful hospital-developed systems into tools that can be reliably adopted across heterogeneous healthcare environments. Absent better-defined mechanisms to support this transition, hospital-developed AI may remain confined to its originating institutions, even where broader deployment might be clinically desirable.

Comparing the current regulatory approaches still reveals a deep divergence between designed regulatory accommodation in the EU and incidental regulatory permissiveness in the USA. In the EU, hospitals are explicitly recognised as regulatory actors and flexibility is structured through institutional obligations. In the USA, by contrast, hospital-developed AI largely operates within a general regulatory framework that does not directly address its institutional context.

As indicated in the above, the significance of this divergence is likely to become more apparent as both systems evolve. Ongoing reforms in the EU, alongside the still fragmented and developing AI governance landscape in the USA, will test whether structured institutional oversight translates into more consistent and accountable use, or whether more permissive approaches better support timely development and diffusion. Our argument has, self-consciously, focused on regulatory design choices and possible implications not outcomes. This article does not provide empirical evidence that either regulatory model causes better real-world clinical, innovation or diffusion outcomes. The empirical basis for assessing these trade-offs remains limited. Comparative evidence on the volume, development timelines, governance practices and clinical performance of hospital-developed AI systems, as well as on the pathways through which such systems diffuse beyond their originating institutions, would be useful to inform the picture. Even with such evidence, isolating the causal effects of regulatory design from other differences—hospital organisation, reimbursement and national health policy—would remain difficult. Still, reflecting on the underlying design choices helps clarify what each system is trying to accomplish.

What is clear is that regulatory recognition of hospitals as a distinct actor is a consequential design choice. The central challenge for policymakers is therefore not only how much flexibility to allow but how to ensure that such flexibility is meaningfully governed as innovation increasingly originates within healthcare systems themselves. This may require, for example, clearer documentation and transparency obligations for in-house systems, more structured pathways for transitioning successful tools from internal use to broader deployment and more explicit oversight where hospital-developed systems begin to circulate across institutions.
